title: Mattress stitch seam
subtitle: Joining two knitted pieces with a flat, invisible seam along the row edges.
excerpt: Mattress stitch creates a nearly invisible seam by picking up the horizontal bar between the first and second stitches on each piece in turn. It is the standard seaming method for joining the side seams and sleeve seams of knitted garments.
sourceNotes: Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), seaming chapter. Weldon's Practical Knitter finishing notes describe the pick-up seam in similar terms. Widely documented in UK and US knitting publications as the standard seam for vertical edges.
heroPrompt: Close-up of a darning needle weaving through the bar between stitches on two adjacent pieces of stocking-stitch fabric, forming a seamless join.

glossaryTerms.definition: A seaming method in which a tapestry needle picks up the horizontal bar between the first and second stitches of each piece alternately, pulling the edges together to form a flat, nearly invisible join.
The edge stitch at each side of a flat knitted piece, often slipped or worked in a consistent way to produce a neat, even edge that is easier to seam.

content.text: joins two vertical edges by picking up the small horizontal bar that sits between the first and second stitches on each piece. Pulled gently, these bars draw the edges together from inside, leaving the right-side fabric smooth and continuous. It is the seaming method of choice for side seams, sleeve seams, and anywhere the join should be invisible from the outside. Difficulty: beginner.
Two blocked pieces with matching row counts
A blunt tapestry needle (also called a darning needle)
A length of the same yarn used for knitting, or a matching yarn in a finer weight
Lay both pieces flat with right sides facing up, edges aligned side by side. Thread the tapestry needle with a long length of yarn and knot the tail.
Anchor the yarn by passing the needle under the cast-on edge of both pieces and pulling through. This aligns the starting points.
On the right-hand piece, find the horizontal bar between the first and second stitches in the first row. Insert the needle under this bar from bottom to top and pull the yarn through.
Move to the left-hand piece. Insert the needle under the corresponding bar in the same row on the opposite piece, again from bottom to top.
Continue alternating between the two pieces. Pick up one bar on each side for every row. Pull the yarn through gently after every 4-5 picks.
After every few picks, pull the yarn firmly but not tightly to draw the seam closed. The edges should pull together and disappear, leaving a smooth surface on the right side.
Continue to the cast-off edge. Secure the yarn by passing the needle under the seam yarn several times, then cut close to the work.

Mattress stitch is the standard method for side seams and sleeve seams on sweaters, cardigans, and vests knitted flat. It also joins the side seams of knitted cushion covers, bags, and any flat piece assembled after blocking. The
at each edge of the piece is consumed into the seam, so the finished width matches the pattern's stated blocked width.

items.symptom: The seam pulls in and the fabric puckers
items.cause: The yarn is being pulled too tightly after each pick
items.fix: Use a lighter tension. After every few picks, pull until the edges just meet without compressing the fabric. The seam yarn should be invisible, not taut.

items.symptom: A ridge is visible on the right side
items.cause: The needle picked up too many bars at once, or caught the selvedge stitch rather than the bar behind it
items.fix: Pick up only one bar per row, and make sure the needle goes under the horizontal bar between the first and second stitches, not through the edge stitch itself.

items.symptom: The two pieces do not match row for row and the seam skews
items.cause: Different numbers of rows on each piece, or started at different points
items.fix: Block both pieces to the same row height before seaming. Count rows on both pieces if in doubt.
